topics.title: k 9 Breaking Math II
topics.text:
This post is continued from "Breaking Math I". To view it please click this.





I can prove why any positive number can equal its negation. Same as "Breaking Math I", we will start with something that we are sure about. Many mathematicians have been arguing about the true identity of $\sqrt{-1}$. Some say the that $\sqrt{-1}$ is undefined, but we know that there is a number, $i$ available for us to use. Although there is $i$, we will be using the term $\sqrt{-1}$ today. Using this we can actually prove 2 things today: the real identity of $\sqrt{-1}$ and that any positive number can equal its negation.



$\sqrt{-1}$ $*$ $\sqrt{-1}$ = $-1$



We know that when we multiply radicals, there is a shortcut. We can combine the radicals and multiply the terms inside.



$\sqrt{-1 * -1}$ = $-1$





The above equation is the result when we combine the radicals. Then, we will follow the operations below:



$\sqrt{1}$ = $-1$

$1$ = $-1$



Woah. Something is not right, you say. But when you look closely, nothing is incorrect in the operations. The $1$ inside the radical is from $-1 * -1$. "But this is IMPOSSIBLE!!!" you protest. "How did this happen?" Well, how about you tell me? Gather information from "Breaking Math I" and this post and prove that a positive number cannot equal its negation.



This post continues to "Breaking Math III"

topics.title: Breaking Math IV
topics.text:
I didn't really have a title for this so.show 1^2=0. Sorry a lot
 But what I really wanted to get into is the symmetry between geometry and algebra. We have the cartesian graph and different graphs as such. This symmetry was discovered a while back, but I wanted to talk about something difference. Take a look at this problem (I'm generalizing it). We have $AB$. We can draw $AC$ and $BD$ such that they are parallel and if we draw $CD$ does not intersect with line $AB$. We have lines $CB$ and $DA$. They intersect at $E$. Let's draw a line from $E$ to $AB$ at point $F$ such that this line is parallel to $AC$ and $BD$. Find the length of $EF$. You have probably seen this problems, and the answer is rather a work of similar triangles. But can you see the connection with the problem with the probem, "It takes me $x$ time to paint a fence. It takes you $y$ times to paint a fence. How long for both of us to paint it." I'm sure the connection has been made many times but I really wanted to explore this idea of symmetry between subjects.

topics.title: Spooky Devil's Night Problems!!! - Halloween Edition
topics.text:
It's almost Halloween, but today, it's Devil's Night  :diablo:  :furious:

Time for some insane math problems, let's go!! (Heck, this might even serve as some AMC 8 practice for all you middle school or below peeps out there)



1. Dulce the Devil can eat $10$ mints in exactly $11$ days. Each day, her cousin adds one more mint to her kitchen. On Monday, Dulce starts out with $2018$ mints. On what day of the week will she then finish eating all of the mints for the first time (before her cousin comes back the next day to give her one more)? Assume her eating rate is uniform.



2. The night before Halloween, namely Devil's Night, legend says that the Higgsbury the Devil comes out to light Jack O' Lanterns on fire. He works together with his servant Hades to light $1000$ of them. He can light $60$ every hour, Hades lighting $200$. When they have finished lighting all of them up, how many more Jack O' Lanterns has Hades incinerated than Higgsbury?



3. Adam the Devil is choosing a number between $a$ and $b$, Bary the Devil is choosing a number between $a$ and $c$, and Carlos the Devil is choosing a number between $a$ and $d$, where $0<a<b<c<d$ are integers. Daniel the Devil wants to choose a number $n$ such that he can maximize the probability of him being as close as possible to the arithmetic mean of the numbers Adam the Devil, Barry the Devil, and Carlos the Devil chose. Assuming that each person chooses the number from their interval uniformly at random, what is the value of $6n$? Answer as a function of $a$, $b$, $c$, and $d$.



For each of these problems, the use of a calculator is permitted (although you may want to do these without one if you're preparing for the AMC 8 :)). Search the "spooky problems" tag for more!

IT’S HALLOWEEN PEOPLE!! (and abominations from places I can’t name.) My problem kind of follows the same theme as mathcampion1, but the problem is easier…?



A couple of people bump into each other on Halloween 2018. One is a stormtrooper, another is dressed up as a banshee, the tall dude looks like Michael Myers (or it might be the real one) and the final person is dressed up as Fluffy the town cat. (Fluffy was the candidate that beat Sthenelus in the public vote for the throne of Mycenae, along with Mickey the Mouse.)



To make this problem interesting and longer, the four kids (Michael dude might be considered an adult) got into an argument about whether Hershey’s or Reese's was better. So they decided to settle this in a 4 way nerf gun battle to see who’s verdict was the best.



Suddenly all four became real civilized and came up with a set of rules. (Because all nerf gun battles are civilized.) If you get hit, YOU’RE OUT. The last person unbulletified WINS.



The dude that looks like Michael always hits his target. (Since Horror movie villains always has to one up those really dumb protagonists.) Fluffy has a pretty good aim with a 7/9 chance of hitting his target. Banshee person has a bad aim with only a 50% chance of hitting their target. (oof) And finally Stormtrooper boi has a poor aim with a 1/100 chance of hitting someone. (OOF) Since Stormtroopers have terrible aim, the kid dressed up as one goes first, followed by Fluffy, and finally Michael. What is stormtrooper kid’s best strategy of not getting yeeted on, and what is his probability of winning?

3. A solid cube is formed from $125$ unit cubes. A set of unit cubes will be removed, leaving behind a smaller solid cube. In how many different ways can this be done? (For example, there are $8$ ways to remove $61$ unit cubes from the original $5\times 5\times 5$ cube to leave behind a cube with edges of $4$ units.)



4. For how many positive integers $50\leq n\leq 99$ is the sum of the first $n$ positive odd integers a factor of $n!$?



5. Using $4$ distinct positive integers, we find the five distinct sums of the six possible pairs of these integers to be $27,41,44,47,$ and $61.$ One of these sums occurs twice. What is the smallest of the four integers?

topics.title: 400th post
topics.text:
Yay, its been 400! they really seem to go so fast......

First, here are some things about 400:

It is a perfect square of 20.

It has 15 factors.

It is divisible by the sum of its digits.

It is $1+7+49+343$, the powers of seven.

And some problems:

1. Rachel has 400 glops in the Martian currency system. 5 glops are 6 blops, and 10 blops are 20 slops. She wishes to buy a cow for 400 slops. How much change will she have if she pays with everything she has? (answer with glops and blops.)

2. How many squares are between $400^2$ and $2^{400}$?

3. On the Moon, explosions are measured in kabloowies. Mack decides to detonate 200lb of TNT. This results in an explosion that is 400 kabloowies. If a paper sheet can only withstand 0.5 kabloowies, and a sheet of metal is 400 times stronger, how much TNT does Mack need to explode a metal wall if it is equivalent to 400 sheets?
